newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France says Iraqis may not get goods until May.
newsitem.headline: France says Iraqis may not get goods until May.

text.p: France said on Thursday that food, medicine and other necessities might not reach the Iraqi people until May because of delays in the so-called oil for food program.
"This situation would be unacceptable," Herve Ladsous, France's charge d'affaires, told an informal Security Council meeting according to a statement given to reporters.
He said that council members should do everything possible to ensure that goods be distributed as quickly as possible and contracts be approved without delay by the council's sanctions committee.

Ladsous noted that the committee had instituted new procedures and that about a dozen contracts on hold had just been approved. These contracts were for soap and detergent and had been blocked by the United States until it was sure enough U.N. monitors were on the ground to ensure distribution.
He also said Iraq over the last three months had acted responsibly and its attitude merited recognition.

At issue is the oil-for-food plan allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to purchase necessities for its people under sanctions since Baghdad invaded Kuwait in August 1990. The plan went into effect December 10 but no goods have reached Iraq yet.
The council has to decide before June 10 whether to continue the program but first needs to evaluate if the present arrangements are working.
Part of the delays were attributed to stringent procedures set up by the Security Council to make sure the goods shipped to Iraq fall under its guidelines.
In addition the United Nations had to make sure there was enough money deposited in a special escrow account from oil sales to pay suppliers.
Other delays have resulted from ships used by the suppliers taking weeks to arrive, U.N. officials said.

Annan, in a report to the Security Council on Tuesday, said the oil contracts, amounting to more than $1 billion so far, were expedited quickly but the food and other supplies proved far more complicated. He said he did not expect all the goods to be distributed within the six-month period.
